title: Two Texas residents indicted in trade-based money laundering scheme involving used copiers
text:
Two Texas residents indicted in trade-based money laundering scheme involving used copiers
Federal authorities have indicted two Texas residents accused in a trade-based money laundering scheme using used copier sales linked to alleged frauds targeting victims in the United States while funding conspirators overseas. Both defendants have pleaded not guilty following their arrest last month.
Ketan Kamdar, 61, and Jheel Kamdar, 30, both of Katy, Texas, have been charged by indictment with offenses related to a trade-based money laundering scheme involving the purchase and sale of used copiers from American companies to pay operators of alleged fraud schemes in India, according to an Oct. 21 announcement by the U.S. Attorney for the District of Connecticut.
Authorities allege that Ketan Kamdar was the majority owner of Jainam International, Inc., a Houston-based used copier wholesaler. Both Ketan and his daughter Jheel were listed as President in various corporate filings. Since approximately 2023, they allegedly conspired with individuals based in India to launder proceeds from fraud schemes by purchasing used copiers with funds received from their Indian co-conspirators. The copiers were shipped first to Texas and then to India where they were sold for rupees. According to court documents, invoices were fabricated to reflect false sales and misrepresented transactions as sales to companies controlled by the Kamdar family.
The indictment details an incident from June 2024 when a Massachusetts resident was contacted by a co-conspirator claiming affiliation with the Social Security Administration and told that criminal charges had been filed against them. The victim withdrew about $248,000 from a retirement account and deposited funds into five different bank accounts as instructed—over $48,000 went into an account held by Jainam International. The company accounted for these funds through fabricated invoices indicating payments for copier sales from an Indian company controlled by Ketan Kamdar; proceeds were then used to pay India-based conspirators.
Ketan Kamdar and Jheel Kamdar were arrested on federal complaints on September 2; on September 3, a grand jury returned an indictment charging each with two counts of money laundering conspiracy carrying up to twenty years imprisonment per count. The indictment also seeks forfeiture of over $4 million. Both defendants have pleaded not guilty: Ketan appeared before U.S. Magistrate Judge S. Dave Vatti and is released on $1.5 million bond; Jheel was arraigned September 30 and is released on $100,000 bond.
U.S. Attorney David X. Sullivan said, “An indictment is not evidence of guilt... Charges are only allegations, and each defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.”
This investigation involves multiple agencies including the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security Office of Export Enforcement; Federal Bureau of Investigation; Homeland Security Investigations; Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation Division; Defense Criminal Investigative Service; with prosecution led by Assistant U.S Attorneys Rahul Kale, Konstantin Lantsman, and Stephanie T Levick.
The prosecution forms part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative established under Executive Order 14159 aimed at combating criminal cartels operating domestically or abroad—including those involved in human smuggling or trafficking—and utilizes interagency collaboration across federal law enforcement bodies within Connecticut-led prosecutions.
The U.S. Attorney for the District of Connecticut serves all state residents through prosecution efforts supported by about 68 assistant attorneys alongside support staff members under the Department of Justice umbrella, according to its official website.
